sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: Craterellus tubaeformis (Fr.) Quél., formerly also published as Cantharellus tubaeformis, has a grey-brown to yellow-brown cap that starts convex and becomes deeply depressed and funnel-shaped; the centre may open through to the hollow stem. The margin is thin and often wavy. The underside has neither true gills nor tubes: its hymenium forms low, wrinkled folds, branching and sometimes cross-connected, greyish to yellowish and running down the stem. The stem is slender, yellow to orange-yellow and hollow; the flesh is thin and the smell faint.

sections.title: Habitat
sections.text: In northern Europe it often fruits in groups in moist coniferous woods, especially with spruce and pine, among moss, late in autumn. European records also include mixed woods and beech; habitat varies by region.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: VAPKO lists this taxon under its current name; DGfM lists it under the older name Cantharellus tubaeformis. Both include it among recommended food mushrooms. The DGfM specifies that its list covers species eaten after sufficient cooking and in reasonable quantities. This does not confirm the identity of an individual specimen: the very poisonous deadly webcap can grow in the same woodland habitat. Do not eat a mushroom identified only from this entry or illustration; have any harvest checked by a qualified mushroom inspector.

traits: Grey-brown to yellow-brown cap, deeply depressed and funnel-shaped; margin thin and often wavy
Hymenium of low, wrinkled, branching and sometimes cross-connected decurrent folds — no true gills or pores
Slender yellow to orange-yellow hollow stem; thin flesh and faint smell
Fruits in groups, often late in autumn in moist, mossy woods; conifers are frequent in northern Europe
safetyNote: Included in European recommended food-mushroom lists (DGfM uses the older name Cantharellus tubaeformis); the DGfM specifies sufficient cooking. A fiche or image cannot verify a specimen. The very poisonous deadly webcap (Cortinarius rubellus) occurs in similar woodland; have specimens checked by a qualified inspector.
